source_evidence.location: PDF page 1; printed page 5; Section 1.1, footnotes 1–2
source_evidence.anchor: expectation E X ... is, by definition, the Lebesgue integral of the function X : Ω → R; throughout this book, we drop the brackets
source_evidence.observation: The surrounding source treats random variables as real-valued measurable functions on a probability space, interprets expectation as Lebesgue integration, and writes E f(X) without brackets.

source_evidence.anchor: For p > 0, the p-th moment of X is defined as E X^p, and the p-th absolute moment is E |X|^p
source_evidence.observation: The left-hand side in Exercise 1.2.3 is the p-th absolute moment, with p a positive real exponent.

source_evidence.anchor: It is often more convenient to work with tails of random variables, namely with P{X > t} = 1 − F_X(t)
source_evidence.observation: The source's tail convention uses a strict inequality; for the exercise the relevant tail is P{|X| > t}.

source_evidence.anchor: Let X be a non-negative random variable. Then E X = integral from 0 to infinity of P{X > t} dt. The two sides ... are either finite or infinite simultaneously
source_evidence.observation: The preceding integral identity applies to nonnegative random variables and is the inherited result used with |X|^p.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 4; printed page 8; Section 1.2, Exercise 1.2.3
source_evidence.anchor: Let X be a random variable and p ∈ (0, ∞). Show that E|X|^p = integral from 0 to infinity of p t^(p−1) P{|X| > t} dt whenever the right hand side is finite
source_evidence.observation: The selected claim quantifies over an arbitrary random variable X and every positive finite real p, assumes finiteness of the displayed tail integral, and concludes the displayed equality.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 4; printed page 8; Exercise 1.2.3 hint
source_evidence.anchor: Use the integral identity for |X|^p and change variables
source_evidence.observation: The hint confirms that the absolute value and p-th power are essential and that the factor p t^(p−1) arises by change of variables; the hint is proof guidance, not an additional conclusion.

ambiguities.issue: The source does not specify a pointwise convention for t^(p−1) at t = 0 when 0 < p < 1.
ambiguities.evidence: [PDF p.4 / printed p.8, Exercise 1.2.3] The exponent range includes 0 < p < 1 while the integral is printed with lower endpoint 0 and integrand t^(p−1).
ambiguities.impact: Under the standard Lebesgue or improper-integral reading, the value assigned at the singleton endpoint does not affect the integral, but a formal statement may need an explicit convention or an integral over (0, ∞).

ambiguities.issue: The selected exercise explicitly scopes its assertion to a finite right-hand side, although the preceding integral identity discusses both finite and infinite cases.
ambiguities.evidence: [PDF p.4 / printed p.8, Exercise 1.2.3] It says “whenever the right hand side is finite”; [PDF p.3 / printed p.7, Lemma 1.2.1] says its two sides are finite or infinite simultaneously.
ambiguities.impact: The literal contract requires only the finite-right-hand-side case. Treating the exercise as an unconditional equality of extended nonnegative quantities would be a plausible strengthening inferred from the preceding lemma, not an explicit requirement of the selected sentence.

contract_plain_english: [PDF p.4 / printed p.8, Exercise 1.2.3] For any real-valued random variable X and any positive finite real p, if the integral of p t^(p−1) times the strict tail probability P{|X| > t} over t from 0 to infinity is finite, then that integral equals the absolute p-th moment E|X|^p. The absolute value permits X of either sign, and no distributional or independence assumptions are made.
